speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Right Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of and concurrence in amendments made by the senate to Bill No. 34, an act respecting penitentiaries.
He said:	The senate have approved this
bill, adding two amendments. The first is to section 5, by adding a subsection 2 reading:
(2) Nothing in this act shall be deemed to extend or apply to the exercise of the royal prerogative of mercy, or to the remission service of the Department of Justice, or to alter or affect or to authorize any altering or affecting of that direct control of that service by the minister which now exists.
I have no objection to accepting the amendment, which however I did not think necessary. It has never been the intention in any way by this bill to affect the present situation in regard to the prerogative of mercy. I took the trouble to say that anything along that line will have to be considered and be the subject of further legislation if it is deemed advisable.
The second amendment is to section 11, which gives to the commission the power to appoint the guards, trade instructors and subordinate officers. The senate have added these words: "upon the recommendation of the warden." By the old statute those guards were appointed by the superintendent upon the recommendation of the warden. My purpose was rather to give full control to the commission, but the senate have thought fit to add the words "upon the recommendation of the warden , and I am quite willing to accept the amendment.
Motion agreed to; amendments read the second time and concurred in.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to suggest to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) that he make some concession, however slight it may be, to the intelligence of the farmers of Ontario. If they want to feed barley, they will feed it. If they want to sell it to the United States, they will sell it. If they want to buy com for feed purposes, let them buy it. I think we can trust to their decision in the matter without any advice from the hon. member for Qu'Appelle or even from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) or the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley). I should like to see a more generous latitude allowed in connection with some of these things. Although the farmer may not conform to some of our ideas, when it comes to running his own farm under the conditions which exist he is, to use a familiar phrase, master of his own fate. He will decide these questions just as intelligently himself as when he receives the advice of members of parliament, who may be here in this chamber regardless of whether or not they are farmers. The only thing we need to do for the farmer is to give him freedom. The only thing which he needs is the thing which we deny him. The more generous measure of freedom he gets, the better and happier he will be. The greater measure of freedom that is given him, the less trouble this government will have in connection with unemployment, loss of revenue on the national railroad and other problems which we are trying to solve by getting in the way of the only thing that will solve them, the wisdom and common sense of the producers of the Dominion of Canada.

I do not think that legislation to permit the importation of corn for feed purposes will benefit the farmers of this country, neither do I think it is wise or in their interests to lower the duty from 20 cents to 10 cents per bushel. I have been in the live stock business and I know that there is no feed that will make a fine quality of bacon more rapidly than wheat, barley and oats. Such bacon is much superior to corn fed bacon. Our great difficulty has been to sell our wheat. In 1932 we obtained from Great Britain a quota of 180,000,000 pounds of bacon, which we have never been able to fill. If the farmers of the west would mix their wheat, barley and oats together and produce more of the bacon the British market is wanting, they would be able to use a considerable portion of their wheat. I do not think it is in the interests of our farmers to encourage the importation of corn for feed purposes.

The hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) appeals to hon. members to use their intelligence with respect to this matter. I may say that I was thinking somewhat of the tastes of the animals we produce in western Canada, those good steers which the farmers in his district go out west to buy to bring down here to feed. These animals have a taste for western barley, and when farmers go out west to get these cattle, I think it would be advisable that they bring back a carload or so of barley to feed. These cattle prefer western barley even to Ontario corn.

I suppose it would be very difficult to make changes in the tariff to suit every province, but I think I speak for the other British Columbia members when I say that this reduction in the tariff on corn is welcomed in British Columbia by the dairymen and poultrymen. I do not know how many times I have had to rise in my place to contradict the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) when he has spoken about barley for feed. He quoted Mr. Willis, but he is no authority, especially on poultry. He need not come out to British Columbia to preach feeding barley to poultry. There are two reasons why that is not feasible. First, the freight rate from Manitoba to British Columbia is too high. Second, barley is not as palatable poultry feed as is corn. If you throw down corn and barley to poultry, the barley is the last grain they will pick up. Any poultryman who knows his business at all would never substitute barley for corn. I am pleased that the tariff is being changed to equalize the importations of all varieties of corn. It was a sore point to people in British Columbia that corn for distillation or starch purposes should enter free when corn for poultry feed was charged a duty. It is unfortunate that one small section of Ontario should attempt to be a guide for the rest of this country, even if they do beat us out as far as numbers are concerned. Coming from British Columbia, I welcome this reduction in the tariff.

It would be most unfortunate if the observations of my hon. friend should go without correction. He probably is not aware that the appreciation which he has just expressed of the reduction in the tariff has been directed to a tariff which does not affect the poultry feeders of British Columbia It is chiefly South African corn that comes into British Columbia. This has been so ever since the Ottawa agreements, which the hon. member condemned so much. The corn which

However, as representing the constituency in Canada where cut flower growing is perhaps most prevalent, I feel I should not let this opportunity pass without protesting against the reduction of 15 per cent in the duty. The reduction under the budget of 1930 left the duty at 40 per cent. Of course a countervailing provision with regard to the United States tariff was incorporated at that time. May I say at once that
whatever decision I may have made nine or ten years ago on a particular item, particularly one so difficult as this, and which brought me a lot of good-humoured chaffing from hon. members opposite, not only in the house but during the subsequent election, I do appreciate the importance of this industry. After all, the industry produced last year two million dollars' worth of goods. It is, within limits, a legitimate industry. There are certain limits beyond which in a climate such as this it is obviously not economical, but within the limits in which it is now being operated by Canadians who are interested in it I believe it to be worth while, as I did then.
Last year our total importations from the United States were of the value of $152,000, while our total production was, as I said, approximately $2,000,000; and we exported to the United States $21,000 worth. That was against a duty entering the United States of 40 per cent. Under the new treaty the rate is 25 per cent each way, and I am frankly hoping, although one cannot be certain in connection with such a product, that the tremendously larger size of the United States market and its proximity to a considerable part of our industry will enable our growers to profit through the reduction in the United States rate at least as greatly and I hope more so than the United States grower will profit by the reduction of our rate to 25 per cent. After all there is a tremendous market in the United States immediately adjacent to our border, and our industry is close to the border. It is true that the facilities for producing this class of goods are much greater in the United States than they are here, and it is a very difficult matter upon which to arrive at definite and positive conclusions. As my hon. friend points out, the industry is anxiously awaiting the working out of the new rate of 25 per cent each way.

The ordinary dumping provisions of the Canadian customs law will of course apply in the case of any dumping from anywhere. I am not aware of there being anything in the British law which protects the grower there with respect to dumping, or in the United States either for that matter.

The potato question generally illustrates what a difficult country Canada is to govern. In the maritimes, particularly in Prince Edward Island and I think in New Brunswick, potatoes are one of the principal money crops. The production of potatoes for export is a means of livelihood for a very large proportion of the people of those two provinces, not to speak of parts of Nova Scotia and certain sections of Ontario and Quebec. In working out this very difficult matter, and trying to get the maximum advantage for those who must export, we endeavoured to see to it that the productive months in Canada should be safeguarded to the utmost extent. I have before me a careful review of the imports of potatoes into Canada from the United States during the last eight years. During that period the average of the imports would be in the neighbourhood of 160,000 hundredweight annually. An average of 78 per cent of the potatoes imported came in during the months of June and July, running as high in some years as 87 per cent of the total. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps I should explain why that rate was not changed, because it applies to a number of other items. The principle on which the United States works in negotiating trade agreements is called the doctrine of the principal source of supply. No commodity is included in an agreement with Canada of which Canada is not the principal source of supply. It is a very logical principle to adopt, having regard to the legislation under which the United States operates with respect to trade agreement matters. For instance, in connection with canned beans, if they gave a concession to Canada, which is not the principal supplier, that concession under the most favoured nation arrangement would go automatically to whatever nation was the principal supplier, and would thus prejudice the United States in possible negotiations with that nation. I may say that while we have no such legal restriction so far as Canada is concerned we do endeavour to keep the same principle in mind when we are negotiating. It would be absurd to give a concession to one country which was a small supplier of a commodity in a trade agreement in which reciprocal advantages were exchanged. It would mean giving a minor advantage to that country and a major advantage to some third country which in the nature of things was the principal supplier of the commodity in question.

In moving the second reading of this bill, as to-day is the anniversary of a great saint and a great man, and a notable day to a great many people of the Irish race in this country, I wish to compliment you, Mr. Speaker, as the representative of another great people, the people of the glorious land of France, towards which the eyes of the whole civilized world were turned during the great war, who suffered pain, sacrifices, sorrow, anguish and great privations and the story of whose endurance, bravery, and glorious service to humanity will live in the annals of patriotism forever. The people of Ireland were a downtrodden people for a great many years. I wish to pay tribute to you, sir, for your conduct of the public business in the interests of the people of Canada.
In moving the second reading of this bill let me say that it does not in any sense involve the expenditure of money, because it is only enabling and permissive legislation. It gives power to the governor in council if he sees fit to refer any matter of national importance to the people. This house, and parliamentary institutions generally in this country, have not been treated fairly by some of the press as far as reporting the proceedings of parliament is concerned. I should like to take a couple of minutes to answer some of the criticism which has been directed against this house from outside. As far as the notice or reports given by some of the press to the proceedings here is concerned we might just as well turn the key in the door and hold the sittings in secret or in private. The press has a duty to the public, which with three or four exceptions it is not carrying out,-to give to the people the plain facts of what is being done in this house.
The ballot proposed has been the rule in the municipalities for many years. I see the respected and honoured Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) here to-night. I think he is a taxpayer in the city of Quebec.

You, Mr. Speaker, have been a municipal ratepayer for many years and will realize that a provision for referendum on matters affecting the liberty of the subject and the control and disposition of property is a wise thing. For example, the city of Toronto has a splendid patriotic press, all good papers; they do a great deal for the city and country. I do not wish to criticize in any way the press, far from it; I have on other occasions 71492-1271
in my newspaper bill paid tribute to the press and what it does for the people of the country in peace and war alike. But I recall an occasion in Toronto when five of the six daily Toronto newspapers advocated very strongly the purchase by the people at $32,000,000 of an old electric railway and electric light company's franchise and physical assets which was reported by the investigator to be worth $6,000,000. Had it not been for the voice of one newspaper, the Telegram, and one or two men in the Toronto city hall- I am not saying who they were-the people of Toronto forever would have had to pay carfare at a cost of two tickets for a quarter on the streets of the city. A referendum should have been held on the proposal that the municipalities should buy and control this light and power and transportation, and some of the papers supported the purchase and nearly pulled it oil over the people's heads. But an amendment to the municipal act was sent to the legislature by the city, when my hon. friend, the member for Park-dale was in the city council, providing that no franchise to any light, power or transportation company should be granted by law over the streets of municipalities in the province of Ontario without a vote of the ratepayers That amendment to the Municipal Act, which I moved, passed the legislature and is commonly called the Beck act. If that policy is good for municipalities and provinces, it is good federally. It would have been good in connection with the launching of three transcontinental railways. Some of the old newspapers were responsible for the present railway situation and bungle in this country; they said " Cox could not wait." Had the people then had a voice in that, I doubt if the railway situation in Canada would be what it is to-day. I am not criticizing the newspapers, but in the early days of this century they created-at least most of them did-this folly. There is political wisdom even in what I said the other night that you can never answer a newspaper, because it always has the last word.
The principle of this bill is to trust the people, and let them have a more important place in domestic government. What has become of the old clear-cut doctrine of representation by population, a principle recognized before confederation and a splendid doctrine that did credit to Liberalism. It was a good principle, because it gave the people a voice. I would not have a referendum on questions of defence or war or foreign affairs, that would be a great mistake. The government of the day must take the responsibility in an emergency, as Sir Robert Borden did
Elections-Special Ballot

in August 1914, and the country backed him up. The enemy might be in the country and take possession before you could open the ballot boxes. If a referendum was held, they would sail up the St. Lawrence and destroy our leading cities in eastern Canada. I would hold referendums on great domestic problems such as I have described and on over-government and over-taxation. I think the people know more about our railways than some of the members of this house. It does not indicate great wisdom when we see three or four transcontinental, double track railways, with all their branch lines as condemned by the Drayton-Acworth and Duff reports. If that proposition had been submitted to the people in 1905 and 1909 I doubt if we would have had a second or third transcontinental railway in this country; nor, I believe, would we have had the over-government and waste from which >ve have suffered in the past. In the Drayton-Acworth report it was stated that Canada, with a population of 10 millions, had a railway mileage equal to that of Germany with a population of 67 millions, and of France and England, with populations of 46 and 47 millions. With Canada's 42,000 miles of single track it is now too late to hold a referendum.
A further point is that a referendum would be a check on hasty legislation. It would ensure that vital and important measures dealing with domestic affairs could not be passed by parliament against the wishes of a majority of the electors. A referendum is the most effective way of making the voice of the people effective. In the second place the compulsory referendum would be the greatest possible safeguard against sudden tampering with the constitution. It would be used principally in regard to questions of constitutional change, so would not involve serious changes in the routine of government.
The representative system has completely broken down. British statesmen, though professing to serve their constituents and the will of the people, are becoming more and more independent and out of touch with them, except at elections. They can hardly object to becoming more subject to popular control. Under the referendum it is not necessary for a ministry to resign when one of its schemes is rejected. Thus able men may remain in office even though one of their proposals may be rejected. The heart of the whole policy is often contained in some single resolution or law; and if the doctrine of the mandate has any place in democratic theory, it is applicable on these pivotal occasions. The electors would have to vote for measures and principles, not for men, and this they are perfectly competent to do. At

present they are asked to decide between two or three complicated policies which touch every foreign and domestic interest of the state, without a chance to exercise a critical selection between the good points and the bad. Surely they can decide on the advantages or disadvantages of a single legislative proposal. The merits of voting for men, not measures, are disproved by the steady degeneration in the type of candidates elected. The public think they have a good man when they may not. The reason why voting is so small in many referenda is that considerations of party and personal passion and prejudice are absent. Those who do not vote presumably are indifferent to what may happen, so those who are concerned are rightly allowed to decide.
Then, Mr. Speaker, this would be politically educational, and would free people of the habit of thinking in terms of parties. Measures would then be considered from the point of view of the community rather than of the interests of parties, creeds, sects and classes. The House of Commons would still deal with unimportant measures and would have to draw -up each measure to be referred, settle all the details connected with it and finally present the best result that could be obtained. The adoption of the referendum plan would lessen the evils of the party system, because the certainty that party support meant party victory would vanish. A partial or trial application of the referendum system might be made. It would put more vigour into political life and would give the electorate the feeling that they really controlled their destiny. In some of the states of the union and in Switzerland it has been tried with great success. Far from being an un-English institution, it originated in England in the seventeenth century. Its position in the United States is that of substitute for the veto, which is a cardinal feature of English constitutional theory. The royal veto is now a mere survival, but the need for a sovereign veto remains. No fewer than 1,600 instances are known in America, and undoubtedly if the system had been a failure it would have been dropped. It is an ordinary part of trade union constitutions in England, and has worked well. That is, strikes are nearly always subject to it, and in those cases where it is not used the strikes very often fail because of the discord that follows lack of agreement about the policy to be adopted. In addition it keeps the legislature and individual members in touch with opinion in the country during the interval between one general election and the next.
It is not my desire to criticize the newspaper or splendid public activities of that great

Elections-Special Ballot
and most popular young Canadian, Mr. Mc-Cullagh, or of that other patriot and gentleman who was a great pioneer and who is a very much beloved citizen, Mr. Wright, both of whom are old and admired friends of mine. As I see it these two gentlemen have done a great public service, in one sense, in that they have reawakened and reconsecrated public opinion to paying more attention to the way we are governed and the need of modern reforms. After all is said and done, while the fathers of confederation are greatly respected it must not be forgotten that mistakes were made, and it is the duty of parliament to endeavour to remedy those mistakes, and to bring the conduct of public business up to date.
Our whole system of government seems to be upside down. As I see it one of the cardinal principles of our constitution is that the courts shall be subservient to the legislature. To-day the working man is at the mercy of arbitrary social conditions which are quite beyond Iris control. A century ago we reformed the franchise to secure the liberty of trade and commerce and industry. Later that reform was extended for the benefit of the mercantile industrial classes as against a landed family compact, and still later it was extended to wage earners and women, in order to enlist the aid of the women toward the betterment of social conditions. Our governments have done the best they could, faced with that comedy of errors called the British North America Act, a relic of the ox cart days. We are told that we have to suffer all the economic evils of to-day because of the British North America Act; because certain wise men, whose vision did not extend to the conditions of to-day, unloaded the provincial system upon us as opposed to the federal system which they have in England. Many things we enjoy to-day were unheard of in 1867. Then there were no joint stock companies, no telephones, no power development, no air lines, no radios, no old age pensions, no social insurance, no eight-hour day; nor had they the benefit of many of the great discoveries that have been made in science, physics and biology. Are we to assume that these men who lived in the past left us adequate machinery to deal with the problems these new discoveries have brought us? The authors of the British North America Act did not play bridge or squash or badminton, or go to rugby or pro hockey games, but they left us this relic, the British North America Act. As a result the unemployed have to suffer, and we cannot solve the simplest economic and social questions.
What I should like to see result from this referendum system is a restoration of government of the people, by the people and for the people. The British North America Act is blamed for our failure to solve our most pressing problems, but the constitutional parliamentary, cabinet and law reform problems are the most pressing of all. It is responsible for the failure of any effort on the part of the dominion, the provinces and the municipalities to solve the difficulties with which we are faced while the people suffer untold hardship, misery and want.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say that we in this house are even blamed for our present canal system. I saw an article to that effect in the press this morning. The Rideau canal was financed and built by the British government as a back door to lake Ontario to aid the inadequate defences shown in the war of 1812. The newspapers make a great many statements that are not correct. They published garbled accounts of the debate that took place here just a week ago to-night with regard to constitutional and cabinet reform and the statute of Westminster. I suggest that some of our editors should publish what actually happens in this house and give the people the truth and facts; because we might as well be meeting in secret for all that is said about us by some of the newspapers with regard to our proceedings. And what is going on here under the constitution? In the old days our newspapers published an account of the proceedings of our democratic bodies in federal, provincial and municipal affairs. In the last two cases they still do, but not as to the proceedings here. For example, from what source do some papers principally derive their news concerning Great Britain? Do we get it from Britain direct or from Mr. Chamberlain: I venture to say that a large part of the information that we read with regard to the old land-in some papers there are many notable exceptions-does not come from England but through the papers of the United States. Many of the articles you read in the morning papers in this country have already appeared in some of the newspapers of Cleveland, New York and Washington, in United States press chains instead of direct from London.
Those who criticize the party system do so not without some cause. It has some defects, I admit. It sometimes leads members to forget the basis and functions for which political parties were formed two hundred years ago, for the greatness of the country and the welfare of its people. But when you criticize its faults, do not also forget its virtues and what it has done in the old land and in the empire for good government and for government of the people by the people
Elections-Special Ballot

and for the people. It has given the mother of parliaments the good government it has had and its modern reforms for the benefit of the masses and of the suffering millions and the free parliamentary institutions under which we live to-day, which guarantee us liberty of the press, a free pulpit, liberty of the universities and freedom in the legislatures. Surely that is something we should all be proud of. Parliamentary government may not be as efficient as we should all like to see it, but I urge upon the Minister of Justice, who is respected by the Irish as by all classes, to answer the criticisms that we have heard from within and without. The best way in which those criticisms can be answered is for us to bring about certain reforms that are badly needed. From within, let us reform our parliamentary system, our constitutional system, our cabinet system, our electoral system, and let us have the necessary law reform so as to bring all those departments of our administration up to date, making it more efficient in order to give more expeditious redress for the evils of the capitalist system- a good system if it will clean its house of errors-and allowing us to organize that system so that the workers may share in its benefits. That is so far as criticism from within is concerned. As regards criticism from without, we shall still be where we were in 1812; we shall still be completely dependent upon the motherland for our defence.
I do not wish to criticize the press, because I realize that it, too, has its burdens to bear in a day like this, and must be run from the commercial aspect. In fact, in connection with the newspaper bill I paid my tribute to the press. There are only two agencies whereby the people can be kept informed of our parliamentary institutions; one is the press and the other the radio. Unfortunately however people are too ready to jump to conclusions from what they read and hear over the radio. They have heard that nothing is done " on the hill nothing is done by the House of Commons and the Senate. I suggest that the press should give all the facts. This is the forty-seventh day of the session, but I have not read in one morning paper-and I read them all-an adequate or impartial account of what is going on here. The press owe it to the public to give full information of the proceedings of parliament, because they have a franchise of goodwill from the public. I repeat, I am not criticizing the press. There are two evening papers in Toronto and one morning paper and I fully appreciate the good work they all do. But after all, you cannot answer a newspaper, and they do not give all the facts to the public. What I say with respect to the press here is applicable to

the press of the old land, since the demise of the Morning Post; and in the United States there is the same trouble. The present president has almost no press supporting him.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I move the second reading of the bill. I should like to see it go to the elections committee because there is the great principle of good government involved in it. I am sure it would serve many admirable purposes. It would prevent many abuses, it would be useful to the dominion as it has been to the municipalities, and to the provinces, and it would be in the interests of good government to make some answer to the criticisms that have been levelled against this house and against our parliamentary institutions. Either the Minister of Justice or the Secretary of State should, I submit, consider the question of enlarging the powers of the committee on elections in order to give them an opportunity to study the matters involved in the bill and to take into consideration the question of referendum, which has been so advantageous to the taxpayers in the provinces and in the municipalities; and also other election methods regarding the use of billboards and the radio, with a view to bringing about needed reforms in the interests of the people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the bill is to place upon the statute book certain provisions whereby the government may take a referendum on any question of importance. May I point out in the first place that this bill will not establish a right. The government may at any time order such a referendum, provided it is authorized by an act of parliament; and this has been done before, at least in one instance to which I shall refer in a moment.
Let me say at once that so far as I am concerned I am in favour of the principle of the bill. I am in favour of having on the statute book some provisions by means of which the government may in exceptional circumstances have a referendum or take the votes of electors, properly qualified, on questions of importance. I do not however agree with the mover of the bill that some of the questions to which he has referred should have been submitted to the electors. In the first place, the government should take its responsibility wherever an emergency or a question of importance is concerned involving the general administration of the affairs of the country. In such circumstances, I submit that the government should assume its responsibility, bring down its policy to the house, and let hon. members, duly elected and properly qualified to do so, discuss that

Elections-Special Ballot
policy; and members of parliament should also assume their responsibilities in the matter. In other words, I am not carried away by the modern idea that the government is concerned only with minor matters and that as soon as any question of importance arises it should consult the people and have a referendum on any question that occurs in the ordinary course of administration. I admit that there might be exceptional circumstances in which it would seem advisable to consult the people by means of a referendum, and to that extent I agree with the bill; and instead of leaving it to the last moment it might be advisable to have on the statutes electoral machinery whereby that end would be attained.
I have looked into the political history of the country to find instances of a referendum having been held, and I can find only one occasion on which a dominion-wide plebiscite was resorted to. That was in 1898 when the Laurier government held a referendum on the question of prohibition. The government had a bill adopted by the house during the session of 1898. It was assented to on June 13, the title being "An Act Respecting the Prohibition of the Importation, Manufacture and Sale of Intoxicating Liquors." I have in my hand a copy of that bill. The act became obsolete after the referendum, or the plebiscite as it was called, and consequently it does not appear in the revised statutes of 1927. It not only authorized the government to hold that plebiscite, but it also provided the electoral machinery by means of which that could be done. Section 3 stipulated the question to be submitted, which was as follows:
Are you in favour of the passing of an act prohibiting the importation, manufacture or sale of spirits, wine, ale, beer, cider and all other alcoholic liquors for use as beverages?
Section 4 provided for the proclamation of polling day and section 5 set out those who might vote. Section 6 reads as follows:
For the purpose of submitting the question to the electors, obtaining an answer thereto, and ascertaining the result of the vote, the same proceedings, as nearly as may be, shall be had as in the case of a general dominion election, and the Dominion Elections Act and the North-west Territories Representation Act, and their amendments, and the Franchise Act, 1898, shall, subject to the provisions of this act, and of any regulations, orders or instructions made or given by the governor in council thereunder, apply, mutatis mutandis, to the conduct of such proceedings, and with respect to the powers to be exercised, and the duties to be performed by, and the rights, obligations, liabilities, qualifications and disqualifications of, judges, officers, electors, and all other persons, and with respect to offences and the penalties which may be incurred.
Perhaps I may be pardoned for placing these questions on Hansard, but this is an act which cannot be found readily to-day outside of the library. I thought that hon. members would like to know how the plebiscite was taken at that time. The legislation provided for the taking of the vote, how the ballots should be marked, and the returns made. Hon. members will remember that although that plebiscite gave a majority in favour of prohibition, it disclosed a great divergence of opinion throughout the country, and the government hesitated to act according to the results. Perhaps I might pause here to draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that even this way of legislating is not always the best, nor is it necessarily productive of good results. What the government did was to place the Canada Temperance Act upon the statute books at a later day, which act is still on our statutes. It provided for local referendums, if I may use that term, leaving it to each territory to decide whether they wanted to come under the act Although this act is still on our statute book, it is in force in only three parts of the country, in Manitoulin Island, in the province of Ontario; Thetford Mines in Quebec and in Lisgar and Marquette in Manitoba. I am informed that some two hundred local elections have been held since the act went into force. Certain parts of the country expressed a desire to come under the act, and later on asked that it be allowed to withdraw from its operation.
This bill proposes to enable the government to proclaim the taking of a vote or referendum on certain questions. That right is already in existence and has been exercised by a former government, which passed legislation, as I have indicated, to permit balloting on a particular question. Never to my knowledge has there been a general disposition given to a government, as is proposed to be given by this bill; there has always been in contemplation a special question upon which a referendum was to be held. I do not think this bill is sweeping enough in its provisions. It is limited in its scope by sections 4 and 5. Section 4 states that the holding of a poll and the taking of a vote under this act shall be on the day fixed for the holding of a general election. That means that this bill could not be applied in an emergency or in respect to .any question of national importance which might arise during the course of a parliament. Apparently it is meant to apply to questions upon which parliament would not care or dare to take an attitude, something which the members would rather have referred to the electorate at the same time as a general election is held. Then section 5 states:
Elections-Special Ballot

The provisions of the Dominion Elections Act, 1938, and regulations made thereunder in so far as applicable, shall apply to the taking of the vote and making returns in respect thereto.
If the provisions of the Dominion Elections Act are to apply, it would mean that seven weeks must elapse between the instituting of a referendum and the taking of a vote. I do not think I am far astray when I say that if a referendum is needed, it would be in a time of emergency and not at some fixed date every four or five years when a general election is held. Then seven weeks must intervene between the time a plebiscite is announced and the ballot is taken. I think that part of the bill might well be reconsidered. It should be redrafted and studied by the special committee on electoral matters. I suggest that that committee should consider ways of permitting the government to hold a referendum, not on a fixed date when a general election is to be held, but at any time when it might be thought necessary and advisable so to do. The committee should also try to reduce the time between the proclamation of a plebiscite and the polling date.
Under our present electoral laws the voting lists are prepared on the eve of an election. There are no standing lists kept here in Ottawa, and perhaps that is one difficulty to be faced. A period of seven weeks may be necessary in connection with a general election when every precaution must be taken, but it might be possible to shorten that period in the case of a referendum. If the referendum provided for by this bill is not to be merely a means of having certain questions decided directly by the people outside of parliament; if it is intended that this type of referendum shall be a means of reaching the people in a time of emergency, it is essential that the bill to provide the machinery by which a ballot may be taken should not be limited in its provisions as to the duration of time or the date upon which a ballot shall be taken. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I am quite willing as far as I am concerned, to support the bill on its second reading, but if the bill is read a second time I shall move its reference to the special committee.

Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) moved the second reading of Bill No. 36, to amend the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act.
He said: This bill does not affect the principle of the original act in any way. It is simply to give effect to what we attempted to do in 1937, but it was found that the limitation in the act which would end its activities in 1940 was not removed. It is also proposed now to make legislative provision for what was previously done under a vote of a certain sum of money by this house. It has been suggested by those who are checking the expenditures in connection with this branch that it would be much more satisfactory if the powers which the minister now has under regulations and under the vote itself were put in legislative form. For example power is given to purchase land. That simply means that sometimes where we undertake to build dams we have to purchase land, and have done so ever since this legislation was enacted. On other occasions where we are setting up pastures it has been necessary to purchase certain lands, particularly those associated with buildings which may be used in the establishment of pastures. That is now covered by a section of this bill rather than merely by a vote of the house of a certain sum of money for carrying on that work. The same is true with regard to the purchase of machinery and with regard to agreements with provinces and cities and municipalities.
On the occasion of moving the first reading of this bill I intimated to the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) that before further discussion took place I would attempt to have all the information asked for by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) 71492-128J
laid on the table. That information is not all compiled; I had to send to Regina for some of it, but it will be complete at the beginning of next week and can be just as well discussed when the bill is in committee, probably more properly then than now. If that is not satisfactory to the hon. member it can be discussed fully on the estimates having to do with rehabilitation.
In view of the fact that this bill does not affect the principle of the original act, I suggest that it be permitted to go to the committee where its clauses can be fully discussed.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OF OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
The
minister has stated that it is desired to extend the act so that there will be no termination of the operations under it in 1940; also that power be given to the minister to expend sums voted by this house. I suppose that later on the estimates will include a stated sum to be used for prairie farm rehabilitation.
Prior to 1934-35 there was an unparalleled climatic condition extending over a large area in the southern part of Saskatchewan and part of the other prairie provinces, which brought about distressed conditions in that area. For a number of years there were crop failures, and it looked for a time as though that part of the country might be turning into a desert. The municipalities in that area and the provincial government could not cope with the situation. An appeal was made to the federal government for assistance, which I think all will agree was granted, and the situation was met as far as possible. After careful investigation by the Minister of Agriculture at that time the situation was considered so serious that the federal government offered to assume full responsibility with respect to relief, schools, roads, et cetera, in a certain area, taking it over as a federal area. There was correspondence between the then Prime Minister Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, and the premier of the province, who happened to be the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) with respect to that proposal. I have a copy of the correspondence. But apparently the two governments could not agree and that area was never taken over by the federal authorities.
In 1935 the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act was passed, providing for the setting up of a committee, with the main purpose of reclaiming and rehabilitating the area. Many projects were undertaken, including experiments in control of soil drifting, conservation of water, and other worth while projects: the main object being to reclaim the land and rehabilitate the farmers in the area.
Prairie Farm Rehabilitation

In 1935 there was a change of government. The act however continued. It was amended in some minor respects in 1937, but the government of the day has been carrying on that work. I believe they have been seeding large areas to grass in order to try to get it back to pasture. I agree with the main principle of the bill, and I think the government would be well advised to continue the work. The area involved has in the past made a considerable contribution to our export trade. It has had a wonderful record from the production standpoint, particularly prior to 1930, and I believe that that same area may yet regain the position it held prior to 1930 and be capable of producing as much new wealth as any area of similar size anywhere in the west. Certainly if we have a reasonable rainfall for three or four years in succession we shall soon return to that condition.
In the last two or three years those in charge of prairie farm rehabilitation have set up an organization which in regard to size of staff is out of all proportion to the wrork that they are doing. Salaries and expenses are beyond all reason. If you look at pages 56, 57, 58 and 59 of the auditor general s report you will see the names of the employees of this department, together with their salaries and expenses, and I believe after careful study you will agree that the statement I am making is correct.
This amendment certainly gives the minister wide power. He can undertake almost anything he wishes. As he said a moment ago, he can lease and dispose of land as he sees fit. Section 12, which is a new section, states:
The minister may, for the purposes of the act, purchase or rent whatever machinery or equipment may be required in connection with the development, construction or operation of any project, or scheme, and may sell or otherwise dispose of such equipment upon such terms as he may deem desirable.
All this can be done without the approval of the governor in council, which is required under sections 10 and 11.
The minister stated a moment ago that he proposes to give certain information when the bill is in committee, information for which I asked and in regard to which an order was passed on March 6. This has to do with the number of engineers, supervisors and employees of all kinds engaged under the act. I believe we should have that information, as well as a good deal more that I can think of. We should have all the contracts that have been entered into, all the contracts that have been sublet, as well as the leases of land and equipment that have been entered

into. It will be noted that the bill gives the minister power to lease and rent machinery, land and so on. I think we should have this information in order that we may understand how the work is being carried on. We know that in this area-and I believe this applies to almost all of Saskatchewan

there is not twenty per cent of the horse power that is required properly to carry on farming in the district. As I have previously said in this house, the minister would be well advised to consider assisting the farmers in some way in making the first payments on power equipment. I cannot think of any better way to rehabilitate the farmers and encourage them to stay on the land. That may not be possible under this act, but I suggest that any industrial organization carrying on work of this kind certainly would see to it that salaries and expenses were cut about in half. If the minister could do that, it would be a great saving to the treasury, and perhaps some provision could then be made for the assistance I have suggested.
As I said a moment ago, I approve of many of the projects that have been undertaken, particularly those having to do with water conservation. Just here I suggest to the minister that, since certain rivers and streams have been dammed

I think it is under this act that a dam is being constructed near Saskatoon-the board in Regina will have representations made to it in regard to damming the Qu'Appelle river at certain points, and those representations should be thoroughly investigated. At a point on the Qu'Appelle river near the Crooked Lakes there is a place where a dam could be constructed without great cost which would hold back a considerable body of water, and the same thing could be done at other points with beneficial results. If this were done it would also have the effect of creating breeding grounds for wild fowl and game of the kind, and I know the board in Regina will be requested to make a survey of the Qu'Appelle river in order to see if this cannot be accomplished.
The minister has stated that he will furnish all the information desired when the bill is in committee, which I think is the proper time to ask for it. That leaves me with very little more to say at this stage except this: I am surprised that the minister should be willing to accept the responsibility that will be delegated to him under sections 10, 11 and 12. Under the last section he can do many things, involving large expenditures of money, without the approval of the governor in council. I am also surprised that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), the watch

Prairie Farm Rehabilitation
dog of the treasury, should agree to allowing any member of the government to have the power that is vested in the Minister of Agriculture by this bill. I am not for a moment imputing any ulterior motive; far from it, but I do not think these provisions can be carried out without arousing a great deal of suspicion. I am afraid the minister is placing himself in a position which may bring about certain charges, perhaps none of which may have any foundation at all. I am a little surprised to see him go this far; I think it is a mistake. However, when the bill is in committee we may obtain more detailed information.

As far as any statute can be said to be permanent. I want to emphasize the definite change which has taken place in the principle of the legislation. It means that what was originally an emergency measure now becomes a normal statute, similar to any other statute on the statute books. I submit that what the minister is doing by section 2 is not good parliamentary practice. In other words, it is recognized that parliament may authorize the minister or the government to do something under emergency conditions, which under normal conditions would not be sanctioned. I consider we are evading the principle of parliamentary responsibility.
Before I deal with the second section of the bill, let me refer to what the minister said both the other day and to-day. He stated that this bill was to do by legislation that which had previously been done by regulation. The inference was that we were regularizing

speechtext:
But in numerous cases- as in the legislation respecting repayment for seed, legislation respecting the soldier settlement board, and so on-the acts were extended year after year. The farm loan legislation would have expired some years before it was finally wiped out had it not been extended year after year. There is precedent after precedent for parliament extending the time for operation of an act. The time for this act has not yet expired, because under the existing legislation it runs to the close of the fiscal year 1939-40, which we have not even entered. So there is no urgency in that respect.
I know that opposition members are often charged with saying unkind things to a minister when they criticize his legislation, but I hope the minister will not take my remarks in that way, because there is nothing personal in what I am saying. It is simply a question of principle. I do not care how efficient the minister is or may be; I say it is not good legislation to clothe a minister with the powers with which he is being clothed in this bill and in the form of this legislation. That is the whole point of my remarks. I think it is a dangerous course to pursue. As I said the other day, we are handing over to bureaux and boards and commissions the responsibility
for the expenditure of money over which parliament exercises little control. In this case I looked through the main estimates, and I could not find the item there. The minister will correct me if I am wrong, but I suppose it will come in the supplementary estimates- the minister nods his head-in the form of a lump sum, and will be called a statutory vote. That is the kind of thing we do right along. The estimate will come up and someone will question it; the minister will say, "This is a statutory vote, authorized under the farm rehabilitation act," and being a statutory vote it goes through in a lump sum-a vastly different thing from the ordinary procedure where the estimate comes in and is reviewed and the government is accountable direct to parliament for every dollar of expenditure.
What I have said is not with the purpose of reflecting on the minister, but I think this legislation is highly dangerous. It is a bad precedent. It is not an innovation; yet in a way it is a precedent, and it is an unwise course to pursue. We should have done far better to completely revise this legislation, if the continuance of the drought makes it necessary, and bring the whole business of western farm rehabilitation into permanent form so that parliament could review it from time to time just as it does with any other analogous activity such as the grain board or the board of transport-that is, in the regular way.

As the hon. member who interrupted me well knows-

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OF OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
As the hon. member
well knows, the area yet to be rehabilitated in western Canada is of tremendous size, and possibly undertakings which we have not yet even considered will have to be instituted before this area is fully rehabilitated. For instance, the irrigation projects which have been undertaken in the last several years have been excellent to a limited extent, but I believe that either the grassing of large areas and their virtual abandonment as arable areas will have to be undertaken, or in the alternative a much larger and wider type of irrigation will have to be undertaken. Therefore I say that this is not, in the sense in which we usually use the term, something which is passing and just a temporary emergency; it lies much deeper than that.
I do not intend to go to-night into any details of this bill. I intend more or less to fall in with the suggestion of the minister and discuss it next week. But I agree with the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) that this bill ought to be carefully considered by parliament, and that the house should understand thoroughly the wide powers which are being given the minister under the bill.
I know that this problem has been before the house a great deal during the lifetime of the present parliament, and I know that a number of hon. members who are not resident in western Canada have visited the area since they were elected to this house. That, I think, has been all to the good, because there are hon. members from all over Canada who have some understanding of this tremendous problem; and in my opinion the future welfare not only of the area affected but of the entire dominion is involved in the 
question of prairie rehabilitation problem. Unless we can rehabilitate the western plain which has been injured either by drought or by high winds or by soil content depletion or something of that sort, the entire dominion will suffer in time to come.
I would suggest just this, too, that while there may be justifiable criticism of the number of persons employed on this rehabilitation scheme and of the amounts which are expended in inspection and travelling and office salaries and so on, I would not associate myself with the comment-which, although it may have been so understood by some hon. members, was not, I think, so intended- that we are paying too much money to the scientists who are engaged in these projects. As a matter of fact many of the soil chemists and engineers and so on who are doing a magnificent work in connection with these projects are badly underpaid individually.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OF OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext: And overworked.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OF OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.

And overworked. I should like to see, when the minister presents his estimates, a substantial increase in the remuneration which those efficient officials are receiving.
I do not rise particularly to criticize the projects which have been undertaken. I think they run into hundreds, perhaps, as the minister indicated, into thousands; but of that we shall know more next week. Of the projects which have been undertaken, I believe every one has performed a useful service to the farmer or to the community in which it has been undertaken. I want to see this work carried out and continued; for I believe that not only will rehabilitation have to be undertaken as has been indicated, but much more will have to be done. Possibly we shall have to consider how we may best protect the interests of the people who are on some of this land and resettle them elsewhere. We have only touched the fringe of the problem. I hope too that when we do rehabilitate this region we may find places where we may dispose of the produce that will be grown there.
I do not propose to say more except to emphasize that I believe it is a mistake to confer such wide powers on the minister; it would have been better to adopt another method of supervising and carrying out this work.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OF OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.

Every year I have expressed commendation of the forward-looking steps which the government is taking with respect to prairie farm rehabilitation. I believe the proposals indicated in sections 10, II and 12 of this bill

Prairie Farm Rehabilitation
are all necessary. We in our generation must do the planning which the past generation neglected to do with respect to the Canadian west, and these sections indicate that we are preparing to do that. As to whether or not it is advisable to give all these powers to the minister, I am not prepared to make any pronouncement. The powers must be placed somewhere, the activities performed and the projects undertaken; and if the minister finds the responsibility too much for him, he will I am sure in the course of a year or two bring down legislation to confer these powers upon a commission. I have confidence in the minister to that extent. Once more I commend him for his action looking to greater activity in carrying on prairie farm rehabilitation.
Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) ; I desire to say just a few words in reply to some of the suggestions made. Very careful consideration has been given to the salaries paid to officials, and the wages paid to those employed under this act, since the present government came into office, and I believe before. Before we came into office a staff had been employed under the legislation of 1935, and most of those who were in positions of authority at that time are still in the employ of the government carrying on this work. As the work grew it became necessary of course to employ others, and as the expenditure of money increased it became necessary to employ more and more people in the proper expenditure of the money made available by this house. The salaries for the different positions have been referred to the civil service commission in order that *we might be assured that they have some relationship to those of persons employed in similar work in other departments. In April 1938, I think we brought down for the first time our recommendations for increases in salaries, and those recommendations have been so carefully checked that it was only within the last two or three weeks, or certainly within a month, that they have been authorized by the government through the treasury board. We had the civil service commission make the most careful inquiry into any increases in salary that were made, or increases in payments to officials who were drawing salary; and I believe all the care that could possibly be taken in that connection has been [DOT] taken under the direction of the treasury board.
It was stated a few moments ago by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) that very wide powers were given in
section 7 of the original act. That section reads:
The governor in council may make such regulations as may be necessary or expedient for the effectual execution and working of this act and the attainment of the intention and objects thereof.
I cannot conceive of any wider powers being given than were given in that section. It gives to the governor in council power to make regulations, and under those regulations certain powers have been given to the minister. By this legislation council had the right to do what we are now asking parliament to do, namely, to instruct the minister to do certain things, without their having been specifically placed in the legislation at all. There is not a single thing referred to in sections 10 or 11-I am not certain about 12-that was not done under the minister while the previous government was in office; not a single thing can be done under sections 10 and 11 that I have not been doing for the last three years.
At the time the legislation was placed upon the statute book it was thought, as the hon. member for Kootenay East stated, that this might be a temporary measure. But as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well) has just pointed out, I think every hon. member is now convinced that the problem of the prairies was not nearly as "temporary" as in 1935 some of us hoped it might be. We have had another four years' experience with it, and everyone who has visited that section of Canada realizes what was stated a few minutes ago by the leader of the Social Credit group (Mr. Blackmore), that if in the early days the government of Canada had taken more care with the settlement of that section of the country, we should not now be required to do so much of what is known as rehabilitation work. But that care not having been taken then, it is now necessary to set apart sums of money, provide for the resettlement of certain sections, and make it possible for people to continue living in areas that were settled without proper preparation for settlement.
I say, then, that the activities that will be carried out under sections 10 and 11 of this bill are exactly the same activities that we are now carrying out under regulations as provided for in section 7 of the original act. But it stands to reason that officials in the departments checking expenditures desire that some more specific statutory authority be given to the minister than merely the power given by the governor in council under regulations made under section 7 of
Prairie Farm Rehabilitation

the old act. - What we are really doing is asking parliament to enact legislation giving us powers that were given previously under section 7.
For the purpose of this act there was set up an advisory committee as provided for in the original act. speechtext:
Well, that was the argument used at the time. We went into that very fully and the then leader of the opposition was fearful that we would not reappoint representatives of practically the same institutions. I assured him at that time that while some of the individuals might be changed, and while we might not think it necessary to have some of the institutions mentioned represented on a committee that was being set up for the purposes set out in the bill, to all intents and purposes it would be practically the same committee. I have not the personnel before me at the moment, but an examination of it would indicate that practically every institution represented here is represented in the same manner as before, in some cases by the same persons; or is represented on the committee with a slightly different personnel and slightly different set-up. But we have other committees in advisory capacities as well, and these committees will give advice to the minister from time to time. It will be noted that the new section 10 says:
The minister may, subject to section four of this act-
That is, subject to being advised by one of these committees.
-and with the approval of the governor in council, enter into agreements with any of the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan or Alberta or with any city, town or other municipality within any of the said provinces, or with any person, firm, or corporation, with respect to the development, promotion, construction, operation and maintenance of any project or scheme undertaken under and by virtue of this act or which may be deemed necessary or desirable for the conservation of water.
In other words the act sets out exactly what we have been doing for the last four years. Each time we acted we had the advice of the Department of Justice as to whether we were within the terms of the legislation then on the statute book; and on 	.
each occasion we were advised that we were. But we feel that when we are asking the house to make this legislation more permanent than it has been in the past, by removing the date, at the same time we should ask parliament to give us specifically the powers we have had by order in council ever since the original act was passed.
Then section 11 states:
The minister may, for the purposes of the act, and with the approval of the governor in council, purchase, lease or otherwise acquire, or sell, lease or otherwise dispose of, any lands or premises which may be required for or included in any project or scheme, upon such terms or conditions as he may deem desirable.
This leads us back to section 10, and thus brings in the provision with regard to recommendations by advisory committees. In other words, we undertake these activities as a result of their advice and recommendations. Then we proceed under the other section by order in council to do the very things we are now doing. We have simply set out in this legislation the powers which previously were given us by order in council.
In regard to the last section there is just the possibility that there may be some room for criticism. I suppose I am really breaking the rules of the house in discussing this bill clause by clause at this time, but I am doing so only because it has been dealt with in that way by other speakers. There may be some reason for asking that the approval of the governor in council should be inserted in section 12 as well, and as far as I am concerned I have no objection to that if it should be the wish of hon. members when this bill is in committee. There are such things as these to be dealt with, however. For instance, we have to buy machinery for levelling land to be used in some irrigation scheme. We have the land levelled; we are finished with the machinery, which may be of a type suitable for use by people who are on that land. We may feel that rather than move that machinery to a point a hundred miles away where we are carrying on some other project, with all the expense in connection with such movement, it would be better to dispose of that machinery to the people who are going to remain on the irrigated land. So it may be found necessary to dispose of that machinery in that way.

speechtext: It is a dangerous procedure.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OF OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
It may be, but it is something that has to be done if we are not to leave the machinery lying in some fence corner. So the machinery is disposed of and accounted for. The only result if the governor

That is a matter that can be considered when the bill is under consideration in committee. The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) says we may have to get an order in council to sell a wheel barrow, and I suppose on some occasions it might get down to that.
I do not desire to go into committee on the bill to-night, because of an undertaking I gave the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas), who is not in his seat at the present time, but I would ask that it be given second reading now.
