Science service-
11. Entomology, $488,511.
What services are included under this item?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The different services that
are covered in the records I have here are: field crop insect investigations; fruit insect	investigations;	insecticide	investigations; forest insect investigations; investigations on insects and allied parasites of animals and man; stored product insect investigations; insect taxonomy; parasite investigations, and other investigations and activities.
How many persons are employed in this branch?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
There are 207 permanent and temporary employees.
Mr.	COLDWELL:	I imagine	the	grasshopper	infestation is	covered by	this	item.Would	the minister	outline what is	being
done this year in that regard; whether any new methods are being used, and what is the anticipated requirement this year? I ask that question because reports from the west seem to indicate that there will be a serious infestation this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
With regard to the first suggestion, that something be said as to what has been done in connection with grasshoppers. I would say this; that, as suggested by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, there was a very bad outbreak of grasshoppers in the western section of the prairie
area last year both in Canada and in the United States. Along the southern boundary of Saskatchewn there was a breeding of grasshoppers in very considerable numbers, and crops in the southeastern part of the province were destroyed by grasshoppers very early in the season, before the grain had headed out. Towards the end of July or the early part of August the grasshopper moves from its breeding grounds to new fields, and during that period it moves further north and west with the winds that have carried it into other sections of the province. The grasshoppers destroyed thousands of acres of crop all through central Saskatchewan and some areas of Alberta. They continued to be in outbreak form in the prairies and British Columbia during 1938. The outbreak in the prairies, owing to the peculiar weather conditions, was more intense and destructive than expected, with the result that severe losses took place in Saskatchewan, owing particularly to migrations of insects from the United States. An area of 62,000,000 acres, roughly speaking, was infested in the prairie provinces in varying degree. The grasshoppers attack all cultivated crops. The most important losses are to grain and fodder crops in the prairies and to range grasses in British Columbia.
The insects are controlled mainly by poisoned bran and sawdust bait which is scattered in infested fields. Control campaigns were successful in Manitoba, British Columbia and Alberta and northern parts of the infested areas of Saskatchewan. In southern Saskatchewan serious losses were suffered together with peculiar weather conditions. The crop losses in British Columbia were surprisingly low owing to control work. In Alberta the losses did not exceed three per cent of the field crops and were but a small percentage even in infested areas of Manitoba. The crop destruction in Saskatchewan was severe. The outbreak anticipated in 1939 will cover a greater ac age and will be of greater intensity than that of 1938, but a more thorough organization of control activities in Saskatchewan is expected to reduce greatly the losses from these insects in 1939.

As regards the abandoned land in southern Saskatchewan, what steps are taken to look after that area as a breeding place for grasshoppers? Following that question, in order to save time, the minister might give an outline of the steps that have been taken in cooperation with the United States authorities, since migrations came largely from the United States last July and August, along our own southern boundary.

Supply-Agriculture-Entomology
Mr. GAiRDINER:	The United States
government have a very large program of control in the states immediately south of the prairie section of the west. The dominion authorities have been in touch with the United States authorities. I know that the Saskatchewan authorities have been in veiy close touch with them, and I presume those of Alberta and Manitoba have been as well. There is the closest working arrangement between the authorities on the two sides of the line.
With regard to the grasshopper outbreak on the Canadian prairies, it is expected to be much worse in 1939 than it was in 1938 owing to a material increase in the area infested in all three provinces. The infested area in 1938 was 62,000,000 acres, and this is estimated to have increased to approximately 97,000,000 in 1939. The increase in general, however, is in area infested rather than in a spectacular increase in intensity of infestation. That probably is the best comment I can make on the question which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has raised. If there is an area of 97,000,000 acres infested, the infestation is not at all confined to the areas that have been abandoned by farmers. As a matter of fact, judging from the experience that I have had personally, I think the infestation is more likely to be around the edges of fields that are in crop, and not very far removed from them, and probably in areas that were in crop last year. Eggs will be found in the soil in those areas in greater numbers, I suggest, than in the abandoned land. The increase is due in large measure to the unusual amount of migration, both domestic and from the states to the south of us, which characterized the outbreak in 1938. The infested territory in Manitoba increased from some 1,800 square miles to a little over 10,000 square miles. That of Saskatchewan increased from 55,000 square miles to 95,000 square miles.
Mr. MaeNICOL: In 1938?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
That was the increase in infestation this year. The grasshoppers laid eggs over an area to that extent greater than the year before. While the territory involved in the outbreak in Alberta increased from 39,000 to 49,000 square miles, the greater proportion of the infested area is below the severely infested category, and though the severely infested acreage practically doubled during the year, it forms a relatively small proportion of the territory infested. With vigorous control campaigns organized by the provincial governments in each province the loss of crop is expected to be reduced to very small proportions, and

with more effective control of these insects in the United States, the losses due to migrating grasshoppers is expected to be of little consequence. That is the official statement with regard to the matter. The work on the immediate areas is being done by the provinces. The work itself is not being done under the direction of this government, but we are associating all our officials in this particular branch of the department, who are making studies of these problems here and elsewhere, with the activities of the provinces, in order to make the battle against the grasshoppers as effective as possible.

Have the officials any opinion with regard to the common notion among the farmers that if the soil is wet and the spring is late, the cold tends to destroy the grasshoppers' eggs or larvae and therefore ends the pest? I ask that question because I have heard it stated as a matter of fact that in certain areas where there are many grasshopper eggs there was a good deal of rain, and the farmers feel that there is not much that requires to be done because nature will take care of the situation. I should like to have something on the record with regard to that opinion.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I understand that those who have made a study of the problem are pretty well agreed that merely a wet or cold spell does not affect the grasshopper very much. A recurrence of cold spells and then warm spells, that is, rapid changes in weather over a period, does have some effect in reducing the numbers, but a cold wet spell in the spring will not alone affect them very much. The only safe thing to do is to wage battle against them with poison.

I realize that the problem of treating grasshoppers is largely a provincial matter, but in the past, as far as I know, there has been difficulty year after year in getting the bait. I was wondering whether this government is close enough in touch with the supplying of bait .and whether it could help. To be short of bait in the early stages means a tremendous loss a few weeks afterwards. That is a serious matter in the part of the country I represent.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I understand that all the information has been compiled as to how much poison will be required, what will be required for mixing and feeding it to the grasshoppers, and so on. This information is in the hands of the provincial governments. The task of finding funds to purchase what is required is upon the provinces. I do not know at what stage they are now in their arrangements to secure the necessary supplies in order to carry on the campaign.

Supply-Agriculture-Entomology

To what extent has it been found that fall cultivation will reduce the menace? This has been advocated in the past but I have never been able to see much difference between a field that was cultivated and one that was not.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I am informed that fall cultivation has a tendency to reduce the grasshopper movement. The turning up of the soil and the exposing of eggs to the weather and all that kind of thing has a tendency to destroy some of them.
What steps were taken by the department to check the army worm movement in Ontario during the past summer?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
There is the same
activity in connection with the army worm as there is in connection with grasshopper infestation. We give the same service, and the province or the county does the actual work.
I notice there is an increase of $6,180 in this item. I should like to know how many more people are employed in the branch.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
There are statutory
increases for those employed, which probably accounts for a considerable part of the increase. I understand there has been practically no increase in staff.

The importance of this problem should be thoroughly understood. Could the minister give us any information as to the cost last year of endeavouring to control the grasshopper pest, and the extent of the losses sustained by the farmers?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We have not complete records as to the particular fight with the grasshopper now being carried on by the provinces, but a similar fight occurred from 1919 to 1923. It cost $1,700,000, and it is estimated that it saved $80,000,000 worth of crop. This will give some idea of what the result would be if there was no battle carried on.

As an eastern member of parliament it was my privilege to make my first visit to the west this past season. Although I have heard this matter discussed on many occasions, it was the first occasion I had of seeing the destruction which the grasshopper can do. For the first time I saw the tremendous destruction that had been wrought on the wheat crops throughout the west, especially around Regina and in certain other sections of Saskatchewan. This small insect cuts off the head of the wheat just where it buds out; the head falls to the ground, and as there is no way of harvesting it, it is a complete loss.
My observations of the farming operations in western Canada lead me to the conclusion that possibly our friends in the west are trying to cultivate too many acres. If they confined their activities to a smaller acreage they might be able to control the situation much better. From my conversations with farmers I was led to understand that if the poison was put out in time and properly placed, it was quite effective. I consider it is a very worthy work that is being done, but I think the surface has hardly been scratched, having regard to what might be done. We have had to face similar difficulties in the east in connection with the potato beetle. Our potatoes are prohibited from entering the English market because of that pest. However, this has been controlled to such an extent that they are no longer considered a menace. We spray for blight and include in the spray a small amount of poison which controls the beetle situation.
Perhaps I may be permitted to suggest to our friends in the west that there is enough wheat wasted on every farm

this applies especially to those with which I came in contact-to keep two or three families in the east. Many farmers in the west apparently have launched out on an elaborate farming operation. On many of the farms I visited I noticed a lot of discarded machinery which may have cost more than the whole farm was worth. I do not know how this situation can be remedied, but my first impression was that they were endeavouring to farm on too large a scale and were spending too much money in purchasing up to date machinery. They were wasting much of the crop that should have been harvested. Could the minister tell me how many are employed in the entomology branch at Fredericton?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: From twelve to fifteen.

Not long ago the minister tabled his report for the year ended March 31, 1938. On page 85 reference is made to the grasshopper situation, and I should like to quote as follows:
In Saskatchewan and Alberta the prospect is also for less damage than in 1937, although organized control campaign will be required in both provinces,-
That would indicate that it is not expected the damage will be as great in 1938 as it was in 1937. I appreciate that it is very difficult to make any real estimate, but are we to gather from what the minister has stated that the officials of his department believe the infestation will not be any greater this year than it was last year, or that it will cover a wider area?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
A wider area, yes.

Supply-Agriculture-Entomology

Of course, we appreciate the fact that the most effective method of control is poisoning in the early stage after hatching. From the experience we had in our district in August, 1936, I do not think there can be any effective control of an infestation if the attempt at control is left to too late a stage. It all depends on control after the hatching stage. I had an interesting chat with a crop reporter from the United States side, and he informed me, from an investigation he had made of the number of eggs laid in our district, that no matter what the climatic conditions might be in the spring of 1939, we were bound to have an infestation and a hatching that would be very serious if there was no control. It looks as if we were in for another infestation in the spring.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I can only say that I
do not think it is possible to forecast exactly what will happen in connection with grasshoppers in any year, but the best information available is that which has been gathered by persons who have been making close studies of grasshoppers over many years. The areas are all mapped out and indicated, and anyone can get the maps and study them for himself and know pretty well what the infestation is in his particular area. In the area in which I farm, which is just north of where the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) farms, we had not experienced a grasshopper infestation since I have been in that area prior to last year. The grasshoppers were not hatched in that area; they flew in. They came in during the month of August and started in systematically to destroy the crop, and the thing that astonished me was that they did not work in the same way on any two kinds of crop. They cut the wheat off about eight inches below the head. They cut the stem about half-way through, and the stem fell over and finally broke and fell to the ground. They cut the barley four inches below the head. In the oat crop they took the little tendril that holds the oats, nipping this right off just a few inches below the head. The corn they attacked down near the root. They apparently had their own way of doing everything, and they did it systematically.
While my hon. friend may think you can poison them no matter how thick they are, it is very difficult to do much after a certain stage. I thought they had not got after the grasshoppers in the southern part of my riding as strenuously as they might have done. They had had so many crop failures

that perhaps they thought it was not worth while. I went into Oxbow in the midst of the infestation and the gentleman I saw there was the druggist, who had all the poison he needed in his drug store to fight the grasshoppers, and he undertook to kill the grasshoppers in his garden. He said to me that the only green things left in his garden were the lilies in the middle of the little fish pond in his back yard. He took me around to show me how successful he had been, and you could not put your finger on the ground where there was not a dead grasshopper. The ground was literally covered with them, and there was not a blade of green anywhere. The potato tops were eaten off right down to the stem. Then he showed me the lilies, and the tops were covered with grasshoppers. It is an impossibility to get enough poison to kill them off later in the season once they have flown in, but you can control them by poison in the hatching season; in other words before they reach the flying stage. But if the infestation is really bad, it is impossible to kill them all and you have to try to control the movement of them, by spreading poisoned bait. That experience has been going on ever since people have settled in western Canada, and I would suggest that if we were cultivating less acreage we would have many more grasshoppers to eat up the less acreage.

There is another popular notion that a certain parasite destroys the grasshopper, as is the case with parasites of other sorts in other countries, and it is suggested that parasites might be introduced in order to destroy the grasshoppers in western Canada. Is there anything substantial in that theory?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: A parasite has been brought in from the Argentine which the department is working on in the hope that it will assist in reducing grasshopper infestations. This work as yet is in the experimental stage.
Is there any danger of introducing the Australian rabbit?
Have there been any experiments in poisoning grasshoppers by airplanes?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: A commercial firm in Lethbridge has tried that. Apparently the poison can be spread very well in this way. Our officers are keeping in touch with the developments.

Having lived in western Canada right in the centre of the

Supply-Agriculture-Experimental Farms
infested area, I should like to commend the officers of the department for the work they have done in association with the provincial departments in endeavouring to help control the grasshoppers in western Canada. A good deal of information is put out every year with regard to the grasshoppers; in every post office and bank you will find maps showing the infested areas, and informing the farmer in the fall of the year what methods of cultivation to adopt to keep down the eggs or to kill the eggs then in the ground. It is not a hopeless proposition. Some of us think that because there is a wide infestation and a great many eggs laid in the ground for next year, it may mean a tremendous loss of crop.
The minister in answer to a question a moment or two ago said that wet or cold weather did not necessarily stop the hatching of the eggs, or kill the grasshopper. However, I think the hon. member for Wood Mountain will bear me out when I say that one part of his constituency last year had about ten inches of rainfall from the first of April to the first of July, and it is a fact that no grasshoppers hatched in that area, and no damage was done by grasshoppers where the rainfall was until they flew in there late in the season. Therefore, if we get in the infested area more than the normal rainfall, it is reasonable to expect that there will be little or no damage done by grasshoppers this year. Back in 1935 we had many grasshoppers in a great many areas, and the ground was badly infested, but we had a fairly heavy rainfall in the spring of the year, and if the crop can get along to a fairly good height before the grasshoppers hatch out, they cannot live in a dense crop when they are young, and they must get out or die. The result is that if the hatching is not too early, and the crop has got to the point where the field is pretty well covered, the infestation is not very dangerous.
The hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacLean) spoke of the tremendous size of the farms in western Canada. As a western farmer when I look at some of the fields down here I sometimes wonder why a man bothers to try to turn his outfit around in the field. We have a different kind of farming altogether. I think the farmer from eastern Canada knows better than anyone else how to handle his business, and by the same token I believe the farmer from western Canada knows better than anyone else how to handle his, and is doing it in the most efficient manner that it can be done.
The hon. member also mentioned the amount of machinery used by the western farmer. We do not waste machinery in
western Canada. We do not rust it out. We handle such a large acreage that we wear it out in very much less time than is the case in the east. After all, the average farmer in eastern Canada uses a binder on, we will say, 25 to 50 acres, whereas the average farmer in western Canada uses his binder on 150 to 250 acres. Therefore a binder which has been used in eastern Canada on the ordinary farm for about sixty years is equivalent to a binder which has been used in western Canada for seven or eight years, and one can easily see that it might be thought that there was waste where there is no waste.
I want to commend the officers of the department. I have heard criticism before in this chamber about the salaries which are paid to a number of men who are employed in different parts of Canada by the Department of Agriculture. We have some of the most efficient men in that department who could possibly be got in this or any other country. I believe that the scale of pay is, on the whole, a good deal lower than it might be. There is a country to the south of us which to my knowledge has offered on different occasions, to some of the scientists working in our Department of Agriculture, a good deal more money than they received from us; yet they are still holding their jobs here on lower salaries than they could get somewhere else. I do not like to hear criticisms of the scientific men in the Department of Agriculture. The strongest criticism I can make of parliament in relation to this department is that ordinarily we do not spend half enough money in trying to do more, through the department, for the farmers.

speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Experimental farms-
12. Experimental farms administration,

I should like to draw attention to the wages paid to labourers at the central experimental farm. I brought this matter up last year and asked for an increase, and I want to thank the minister. I do not know whether he was instrumental in bringing it about, but they were granted an increase of two cents an hour.
In my opinion there is discrimination between the treatment of the labourers who work in the fields and the barns at the experimental farm in Ottawa, and the carpenters. The labourers are paid around thirty cents an hour, while the carpenters, plumbers, et cetera, get eighty-five cents an hour. Last year the minister claimed that the rate of wage paid to labourers who worked on the farms and in the buildings corresponded to
2040	COMMONS
Supply-Agriculture-Experimental Farms
the wages paid farm labourers out in the country. I do not think that that is a fair comparison, because most of the labourers are farmers' sons and they have to pay their board and lodging when they come in to the city. I feel that they should get the same wage as the other labourers. I understand that at the experimental farm there are about eleven divisions, and in each division there are fourteen labourers, who are paid around thirty cents an hour, about five or six men who are paid $105 a month, three or four lady clerks; and also there are about twelve other men whose salaries run up to $6,000 a year. I do not question the efficiency of the heads of these departments, nor am I asking for a reduction of their salaries. All I am asking is that we give a little increase to these farmers' sons who are working on the fields out there, and in the buildings during the winter.
Another thing I should like to bring to the attention of the minister is that there should be some form of retirement allowance for labourers who have worked at the farm for fifteen to twenty years. I have in mind one man out there who will be sixty-five years of age next November. He has been working at the farm as a labourer for the past twenty-eight years. He started at sixteen cents an hour, receiving an increase of one cent an hour up to a maximum of nineteen cents, and now he is getting thirty-two cents, or possibly for the past year he has been receiving thirty-eight cents. He will be laid off this November. He is a married man with a family and an invalid wife; how is he going to exist for the next five years until he gets an old age pension? There should be some retirement allowance. I believe that some years ago there was a retirement allowance for men such as he, and it seems too bad that after these labourers have put in long service at the farm there is no allowance for them when they reach the age of sixty-five and have to retire.
I ask the minister to consider these two things: first, a more equitable wage for the labourers at the farm-mind you, they are farmers' sons-second, the provision of some retirement allowance for men who have spent many years at the farm and are forced to retire.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
As it is almost closing
time I will reply in a few words. Last year we raised the pay about two cents an hour, which for the whole service amounted to somewhere in the neighbourhood of $50,000 for the class of labour which has been spoken of. There is a limit to what we can do in that direction without interfering with wages 
in the vicinity of where our farms are. To offer a much greater increase would probably interfere to some extent with the employment of labour on farms in the surrounding area. In a place like Ottawa, where our farms are close to the cities, we are governed largely by union wages for carpenters and others, which makes it necessary to pay a similar wage for work done at the farms.

There are a couple of
questions I should like to ask.
